title: NVIDIA Exemplar Cloud: Lessons for Unlocking Full Performance on AI Infrastructure | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA reports that partner AI clusters built from identical H100, GB200 NVL72, or GB300 NVL72 hardware routinely run 8-12% (and in one case 31-53%) slower than NVIDIA reference architectures purely because of compounding kernel, BIOS, hypervisor, container, and NCCL misconfigurations. Four case studies show the specific diagnostic signals and one-line fixes, and tie them to the 95% pass threshold for NVIDIA Exemplar Cloud validation.

insights.claim: Two AI clusters built from identical NVIDIA H100, GB200 NVL72, or GB300 NVL72 systems routinely deliver 8% to 12% lower training throughput than NVIDIA's own reference architecture on the same workload, model, and global batch size.
insights.speaker: Emily Potyraj
insights.so_what: Advertised GPU counts are a poor proxy for delivered AI capacity; neoclouds and enterprises buying compute should contract on measured throughput versus NVIDIA RA, not on accelerator SKU.
insights.quote: We routinely see 8% to 12% gaps between partner deployments and the corresponding NVIDIA reference architecture (RA) on the same workload, same model, same global batch size.
insights.locator: Two AI computing clusters built from identical

insights.claim: Performance loss is cumulative rather than singular: individual kernel, hypervisor, BIOS, and NCCL configuration choices each cost a few percent and compound into a gap large enough to fail validation.
insights.speaker: Emily Potyraj
insights.so_what: Debugging AI infrastructure is an accumulation problem, not a root-cause hunt — favors operators with deep systems benchmarking teams over commodity hosting resellers.
insights.quote: each costing a few percent, that compound into a gap large enough to miss the 95% threshold required for NVIDIA Exemplar Cloud validation.
insights.locator: The cause is often a stack of configuration choices

insights.claim: NVIDIA has instituted a 95% -of-reference-architecture performance threshold that a cloud must clear to earn Exemplar Cloud validation, making measured efficiency a gating credential for cloud partners.
insights.speaker: Emily Potyraj
insights.so_what: NVIDIA is converting benchmark performance into a certification gate it controls — a soft lever over which GPU clouds get to advertise premium status.
insights.locator: The cause is often a stack of configuration choices

insights.claim: Performance gaps rarely surface from a single obvious failure and instead come from configuration details that only become visible under sustained workload pressure.
insights.speaker: Emily Potyraj
insights.so_what: Synthetic acceptance tests at handover will systematically overstate a cluster's real training capacity.
insights.locator: Recent Exemplar training engagements show

themes.theme: Grace virtualization and SMMU tax on MoE training

insights.claim: A GB200 NVL72 partner deployment running DeepSeek-V3 Mixture-of-Experts FP8 pre-training inside a VM produced iteration times 12% to 14% longer than bare metal, while dense Llama 3 70B on the same cluster stayed within 3% of reference.
insights.speaker: Emily Potyraj
insights.so_what: MoE architectures — the direction frontier labs are moving — expose virtualization overhead that dense-model benchmarks completely hide; benchmark suites that only test dense models mislead buyers.
insights.locator: Case study 1: NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 FP8 pre-training

insights.claim: The MoE slowdown was traced to 24% of host CPU cycles being spent in arm_smmu_cmdq_issue_cmdlist, because under virtualization every guest map/unmap invalidation traps the host and serializes through a single Arm SMMU command queue.
insights.speaker: Emily Potyraj
insights.so_what: Arm-based GPU platforms carry virtualization overheads x86 operators have never had to reason about — a hidden migration cost for clouds standardizing on Grace.
insights.locator: arm_smmu_cmdq_issue_cmdlist is the function

insights.claim: Enabling the Arm SMMUv3 Command Queue Virtualization extension (CMDQV/VCMDQ) in the host kernel and exposing it to the guest let the guest issue invalidation commands directly to hardware without VM exits, closing the 12% MoE gap to within reference tolerance.
insights.speaker: Emily Potyraj
insights.so_what: The fix depends on recent QEMU/libvirt and a tegra241-cmdqv driver — operators on older virtualization stacks are structurally leaving double-digit MoE throughput on the table.
insights.locator: The fix: Enable CMDQV/VCMDQ in the host kernel

insights.claim: Workloads that issue many small kernels per iteration are the ones that expose virtualization overhead, because microbenchmarks of single-thread CPU performance showed near-identical results on partner and reference nodes.
insights.speaker: Emily Potyraj
insights.so_what: Kernel-launch-heavy models are the canary for infrastructure defects; pick them deliberately when auditing a cluster.
insights.locator: Nsight Systems traces captured on the partner cluster

themes.theme: CPU power budgets and process placement

insights.claim: Limiting CPU C-states to C1 in BIOS — a common low-latency default — is actively wrong for AI training, because idle cores kept in C1 continue drawing package power and starve the busy cores feeding GPUs of turbo headroom.
insights.speaker: Emily Potyraj
insights.so_what: A setting inherited from HFT/low-latency playbooks costs roughly 4% of training throughput; power budget, not core count, is the binding constraint on the host side.
insights.quote: This is a common “low-latency” default that is actively wrong for AI training workloads.
insights.locator: The CPU on the partner cluster was configured

insights.claim: On the affected H100 SXM5 cluster, busy cores were pegged at 3.0 GHz against a 3.8 GHz rated turbo, and allowing idle cores to drop to C6 freed enough power headroom to recover roughly 4% on Llama 3 70B pre-training.
insights.speaker: Emily Potyraj
insights.so_what: A single BIOS toggle is worth ~4% of a training cluster's output — measurable dollars per GPU-hour with zero capex.
insights.locator: CPU frequency: turbostat -i 1 during training

insights.claim: Roughly 18% of the training process's memory accesses were going to the remote NUMA node, and hypervisor housekeeping threads pinned to the same physical cores as data loader workers produced sporadic 50-100 ms stalls that propagated into step-time tail latency.
insights.speaker: Emily Potyraj
insights.so_what: Multi-tenant virtualized GPU clouds inherit noisy-neighbor stalls that show up as bimodal step time — a signature worth demanding in any acceptance trace.
insights.locator: NUMA-remote traffic: numastat -p

insights.claim: Isolating hypervisor and host services onto cores 0-7 and 56-63 via cpuset separation, plus C-state and NUMA fixes, shrank a 12% gap to 3%, with the residual traced to a separate NCCL tuning issue.
insights.speaker: Emily Potyraj
insights.so_what: Recovery requires stacking several small fixes; there is no single lever, which raises the operational skill floor for competitive GPU clouds.
insights.locator: The hypervisor housekeeping threads were pinned

themes.theme: Fabric collectives and NCCL queue-pair tuning

insights.claim: A GB300 NVL72 deployment with ConnectX-8 SuperNICs at 1.6 Tbps per node showed a 31% training gap on Nemotron-4 15B pre-training that only appeared at 512 GPUs, with healthy single-node throughput masking the problem entirely.
insights.speaker: Emily Potyraj
insights.so_what: Small-scale acceptance testing cannot detect fabric-scale defects; buyers of large clusters need at-scale validation clauses.
insights.locator: Case study 3: GB300 NVL72 with NVIDIA ConnectX-8

insights.claim: Raising NCCL_IB_QPS_PER_CONNECTION from the default of 1 to 4 cut reference-cluster iteration time from about 1.09s to about 0.83s, with AllGather falling from ~375ms to ~262ms and ReduceScatter from ~389ms to ~273ms.
insights.speaker: Emily Potyraj
insights.so_what: NCCL defaults are not tuned for 1.6 Tbps fabrics — the newest network hardware ships with software defaults that under-utilize it, delaying realized ROI on NIC upgrades.
insights.locator: On the NVIDIA reference cluster, the default configuration

insights.claim: AllGather bus bandwidth measured roughly 28 GB/s at default settings versus roughly 61 GB/s with QPS=4 on the ConnectX-8 fabric, more than doubling effective collective bandwidth from a single environment variable.
insights.speaker: Emily Potyraj
insights.so_what: Half the purchased fabric bandwidth can sit idle by default; a cheap audit item with an outsized effect on cost-per-token.
insights.locator: Summary of fixes

insights.claim: Queue-pair concurrency should not be raised globally because it is fabric- and workload-dependent, and on other fabrics or message-size profiles the same setting can add CPU overhead without improving throughput.
insights.speaker: Emily Potyraj
insights.so_what: Tuning does not generalize across fleets, which structurally advantages operators with per-fabric benchmarking capability over those copying public config recipes.
insights.quote: Don’t increase QPS everywhere. QPS is fabric- and workload-dependent.
insights.locator: Lesson: Don’t increase QPS everywhere

insights.claim: NVIDIA deliberately keeps NCCL version changes outside normal Exemplar tuning scope even though a version mismatch measurably explained part of the residual performance gap.
insights.speaker: Emily Potyraj
insights.so_what: Certification scope is bounded to protect deployment stability, meaning validated clusters can still carry known, unremediated software-version losses.
insights.locator: Because NCCL version changes are outside

themes.theme: Container-visible topology and silent failure modes

insights.claim: In a virtualized B200 deployment, training throughput ran 13% to 53% below reference while nccl-tests on the host passed cleanly, because NCCL_TOPO_FILE and /etc/nccl/topo.xml were never propagated into the enroot container.
insights.speaker: Emily Potyraj
insights.so_what: The single largest documented gap in the article came from a missing bind mount, not hardware — a reminder that container plumbing is a first-order determinant of realized GPU economics.
insights.locator: Case study 4: The environment variable that never made it inside

insights.claim: When the topology file path does not resolve inside the container, NCCL silently falls back to auto-detection with no error, making AllGather and ReduceScatter 2-4x slower with no diagnostic signal.
insights.speaker: Emily Potyraj
insights.so_what: Silent degradation means fleets can burn months of GPU-hours at half efficiency without an alert firing — argues for continuous throughput regression monitoring, not one-time validation.
insights.quote: If the path doesn’t resolve, NCCL fails silently with no error making this one of the harder gaps to diagnose without knowing where to look.
insights.locator: Lesson: Run checks from inside the same container

insights.claim: Validation checks must be run from inside the exact container, launcher, and Slurm allocation that will run the benchmark rather than from the host, because host-level health tells you nothing about what the job actually sees.
insights.speaker: Emily Potyraj
insights.so_what: A concrete audit protocol for anyone doing technical diligence on a GPU cloud's claimed performance.
insights.quote: Run checks from inside the same container, launcher, and Slurm allocation that will run the benchmark not from the host.
insights.locator: Lesson: Run checks from inside the same container

themes.theme: Preflight discipline and the economics of late debugging

insights.claim: Preflight diagnostics do not guarantee an Exemplar Cloud pass because some issues appear only under the exact model, precision, topology, container, launcher, and network conditions of the validation run.
insights.speaker: Emily Potyraj
insights.so_what: Certification timelines for new GPU clouds carry irreducible schedule risk, which matters for capacity-ramp forecasts.
insights.locator: At the same time, preflight diagnostics

insights.claim: Workload-level tuning such as pipeline parallelism, microbatch sizing, and communication overlap should be attempted only after platform issues are ruled out, inverting the order most teams instinctively use.
insights.speaker: Emily Potyraj
insights.so_what: Model-side optimization effort is frequently wasted on what is actually a BIOS or container defect — a cost-of-engineering argument for platform-first triage.
insights.locator: Preflight checks before full-scale training debug

insights.claim: NVIDIA is publishing its internal diagnostic patterns, preflight checklists, benchmarking recipes, and a perf-per-TCO calculator so partners can self-test before formal reference architecture validation.
insights.speaker: Emily Potyraj
insights.so_what: NVIDIA is standardizing how the market measures AI infrastructure efficiency — controlling the benchmark is a durable form of ecosystem control alongside the silicon.
